steps.title: Create a CSS file and understand the focus-visible concept
steps.instruction: Create a new CSS file and add a comment explaining that focus-visible is a pseudo-class that helps make focus indicators visible only when needed for keyboard navigation.
steps.hint: Start by creating a CSS file. The first line can be a comment that explains what focus-visible does for accessibility.
steps.analogousExample:
/* This is a CSS comment explaining a concept */
/* focus-visible helps keyboard users see focus indicators */
steps.seedCode: /* Add your comment about focus-visible here */
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS file with an explanatory comment about the focus-visible pseudo-class and its accessibility purpose.
successCriteria: The CSS file contains a comment that mentions focus-visible as a pseudo-class and explains its role in keyboard navigation accessibility.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a CSS file and added a clear comment explaining the focus-visible concept. This sets the foundation for understanding accessibility-focused styling.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the CSS file, but your comment doesn't fully explain focus-visible's purpose for keyboard navigation. Try to mention that it makes focus indicators visible only when needed for keyboard users.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS file doesn't contain the required comment about focus-visible. Please add a comment explaining that focus-visible is a pseudo-class that helps make focus indicators visible only when needed for keyboard navigation.

steps.title: Set up basic HTML structure for testing
steps.instruction: Create a basic HTML file with a button, link, and input element to test focus styles. Save it as index.html.
steps.hint: Use standard HTML tags: <button>, <a>, and <input>. Include placeholder text or labels for clarity.
steps.analogousExample: A link
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Focus Test</title>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add a button, link, and input element here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: An HTML file with three interactive elements ready for CSS focus styling.
successCriteria: The HTML file contains a <button>, an <a> link, and an <input> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the HTML structure with all three interactive elements. This will allow us to test focus styles in the next steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have some elements, but make sure to include all three: a button, a link, and an input field.
steps.feedbackWrong: The HTML structure is missing required elements. Please add a button, a link, and an input element.

steps.title: Add default focus styles for all interactive elements
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule that targets the :focus pseudo-class for all interactive elements (button, a, input) and sets a visible outline style.
steps.hint: Use the selector 'button:focus, a:focus, input:focus' and apply 'outline: 2px solid blue;' to make the focus indicator clearly visible.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Focus Test</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your focus styles here */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add a button, link, and input element here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS file now contains a rule that applies a visible blue outline to buttons, links, and inputs when they receive focus, making the focus indicator accessible.
successCriteria: CSS includes a selector for button:focus, a:focus, input:focus with an outline property set to a visible style (e.g., 2px solid blue).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added basic focus styles that will make interactive elements clearly visible when focused, improving accessibility.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but ensure your CSS rule targets all three element types (button, a, input) with the :focus pseudo-class and sets a visible outline.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule is missing or incorrect. Focus styles are essential for accessibility—add a rule like 'button:focus, a:focus, input:focus { outline: 2px solid blue; }'.

steps.title: Introduce the :focus-visible pseudo-class
steps.instruction: Replace the existing :focus selector in your CSS with :focus-visible to apply focus styles only for keyboard navigation.
steps.hint: Change the selector from :focus to :focus-visible in your CSS rule.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Focus Test</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your focus styles here */
        button:focus {
            outline: 2px solid blue;
        }
        a:focus {
            outline: 2px solid green;
        }
        input:focus {
            outline: 2px solid red;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add a button, link, and input element here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS now uses :focus-visible instead of :focus, which will show focus indicators only when navigating with keyboard (not mouse clicks).
successCriteria: All three :focus selectors (for button, a, input) have been changed to :focus-visible.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully updated the selectors to use :focus-visible. This ensures focus indicators only appear for keyboard navigation, improving accessibility.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've changed some but not all of the :focus selectors to :focus-visible. Make sure to update all three selectors (button, a, input).
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS still uses :focus selectors instead of :focus-visible. Remember to replace all three :focus selectors with :focus-visible.

steps.title: Create a fallback for browsers without focus-visible support
steps.instruction: Add an @supports rule to provide fallback focus styles for browsers that don't support :focus-visible. Place it after your existing focus styles.
steps.hint: Use @supports not (selector(:focus-visible)) to target browsers without support, then define fallback styles inside.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Focus Test</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your focus styles here */
        button:focus {
            outline: 2px solid blue;
        }
        a:focus {
            outline: 2px solid green;
        }
        input:focus {
            outline: 2px solid red;
        }
        /* Add @supports rule here */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add a button, link, and input element here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS now includes an @supports rule that provides fallback focus styles for browsers without :focus-visible support.
successCriteria: An @supports not (selector(:focus-visible)) rule is added with fallback focus styles inside.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a fallback for browsers that don't support :focus-visible, improving accessibility across different browsers.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your @supports rule uses the correct syntax and contains fallback styles.
steps.feedbackWrong: The @supports rule for fallback focus styles is missing or incorrect. Review the syntax and try again.

steps.title: Style focus-visible for form inputs
steps.instruction: Add specific styles for input:focus-visible with border changes and clear visual feedback. Use a distinct color like orange and increase border width.
steps.hint: Add a CSS rule for input:focus-visible inside the @supports block, similar to the button and link styles. You can use border: 3px solid orange; or outline: 3px solid orange; for visibility.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Focus Test</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your focus styles here */
        button:focus {
            outline: 2px solid blue;
        }
        a:focus {
            outline: 2px solid green;
        }
        input:focus {
            outline: 2px solid red;
        }
        /* Add @supports rule here */
        @supports selector(:focus-visible) {
            button:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            a:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            input:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            button:focus-visible {
                outline: 3px solid purple;
                outline-offset: 2px;
            }
            a:focus-visible {
                outline: 3px solid teal;
                outline-offset: 2px;
            }
            /* Add input:focus-visible styles here */
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add a button, link, and input element here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS file now includes a rule for input:focus-visible that provides a distinct, accessible focus indicator for form inputs when using keyboard navigation.
successCriteria: The code includes an input:focus-visible selector inside the @supports block with a distinct color (e.g., orange) and increased border/outline width.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added accessible focus styles for form inputs using :focus-visible. This ensures keyboard users get clear visual feedback.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the input:focus-visible rule is inside the @supports block and uses a distinct color and increased width.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction: you need to add a CSS rule for input:focus-visible inside the existing @supports block with a distinct color and increased border/outline width.

steps.title: Test keyboard navigation focus behavior
steps.instruction: Open the HTML file in your browser and test the focus behavior by tabbing through elements with the keyboard, then clicking them with the mouse to observe the difference in focus indicators.
steps.hint: Use the Tab key to navigate through interactive elements (button, link, input) and watch for the focus-visible styles. Then click each element with your mouse to see that focus-visible styles don't appear.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Focus Test</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your focus styles here */
        button:focus {
            outline: 2px solid blue;
        }
        a:focus {
            outline: 2px solid green;
        }
        input:focus {
            outline: 2px solid red;
        }
        /* Add @supports rule here */
        @supports selector(:focus-visible) {
            button:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            a:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            input:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            button:focus-visible {
                outline: 3px solid purple;
                outline-offset: 2px;
            }
            a:focus-visible {
                outline: 3px solid teal;
                outline-offset: 2px;
            }
            /* Add input:focus-visible styles here */

steps.expectedOutcome: You should see that when using keyboard navigation (Tab key), the focus-visible styles (purple for button, teal for link) appear. When clicking with the mouse, only the default focus styles (blue for button, green for link, red for input) appear briefly, and focus-visible styles don't show.
successCriteria: Tested keyboard navigation with Tab key and observed focus-visible styles appear for keyboard users only
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully tested the focus behavior. The focus-visible styles only appear for keyboard navigation, providing better accessibility for keyboard users while avoiding unnecessary visual noise for mouse users.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started testing, but make sure to compare both keyboard navigation (Tab key) and mouse clicking to see the difference in focus indicators.
steps.feedbackWrong: The testing wasn't completed correctly. You need to open the HTML file in a browser and test both keyboard navigation (Tab key) and mouse clicking to observe the different focus behaviors.

steps.title: Review and summarize focus-visible best practices
steps.instruction: Add a comment in the CSS summarizing when to use :focus-visible versus regular :focus for accessibility.
steps.hint: Write a CSS comment that explains the difference between focus styles for keyboard navigation versus mouse clicks.
steps.analogousExample: /* Use :focus-visible for keyboard navigation and :focus for mouse clicks to improve accessibility */
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Focus Test</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your focus styles here */
        button:focus {
            outline: 2px solid blue;
        }
        a:focus {
            outline: 2px solid green;
        }
        input:focus {
            outline: 2px solid red;
        }
        /* Add @supports rule here */
        @supports selector(:focus-visible) {
            button:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            a:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            input:focus {
                outline: none;
            }
            button:focus-visible {
                outline: 3px solid purple;
                outline-offset: 2px;
            }
            a:focus-visible {
                outline: 3px solid teal;
                outline-offset: 2px;
            }
            /* Add input:focus-visible styles here */
        }
        /* Add your summary comment here */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add a button, link, and input element here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS comment summarizing the accessibility best practices for focus-visible is added to the stylesheet.
successCriteria: A CSS comment exists that explains when to use :focus-visible versus :focus for accessibility.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your comment correctly summarizes the accessibility distinction between focus-visible and regular focus styles.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a comment, but it should specifically mention when to use each pseudo-class for accessibility (keyboard vs mouse).
steps.feedbackWrong: No summary comment was added. Add a CSS comment explaining when to use :focus-visible versus :focus for accessibility.
